    Limits

    Windows 11, RTX 4070 (driver 610.88), windowed 800x600, VSync/MSAA off, start then e1m1 on a local listen server. Fresh process per sample, one retained warmup per engine, 9 measured rounds in rotating order. OS and driver caches warm. Signon 4 endpoint for every engine; a first presented in-game frame probe was used only for QSS-M diagnostics. QSS, FTEQW and ezQuake were not rerun; their original medians (166-1106 ms initial, 221-1009 ms change) are far behind.

    Raw logs, per-step results, scripts, the source patch and tests are in loading-optimization/final-2026-10-06/. Source is not committed yet.

    Tested source change · QSS-M observer HUD cache

    The observer HUD repeatedly searched for an optional weapon picture and resolved nine WAD icons every rendered frame. It now caches the loaded or missing result until a HUD/game reload. A regression test covers missing/present icons, reloads, enabling the HUD, and dropping stale pointers. The change preserves the HUD’s appearance and active rendering settings.

    Test build ZIP
    MapBefore FPSAfter FPSChangeSaved µs/frame

    Two discarded warm-ups and three measured native timedemos per map in each block. ABBA build order at each resolution; map order reverses for the second pair. Six measured samples per build/map/resolution; 360 total passes, 216 measured. Both binaries are MSVC Release x64 with the same runtime DLLs and assets. Sound on, uncapped, VSync/MSAA off; no profiler in either comparison binary. Mouse/keyboard-independent full 360° camera recordings match the original frame counts.

    The cache serves observer HUD and demo playback. These measurements do not establish the same gain for ordinary player gameplay, statistical significance, or a new six-engine ranking. The original lifecycle and release FPS datasets remain intact. The separate test build is available above.

    GPU timing · what remains expensive

    Sampled asynchronous GPU timestamps now distinguish the render interval from CPU time inside frame presentation. On this RTX 4070, the windowed 800 × 600 GPU interval is approximately 27 µs while the CPU swap interval is 230 µs. At 4K the GPU interval rises to 190 µs. Driver/presentation work remains the largest CPU stage at low resolution; at 4K, rendering also matters. The exact driver/Windows cause has not been isolated.

    The gap remains open. The observer cache fix removes redundant work, but the nine-map test has not established a material FPS gain. The tested synchronization, flush, gamma-path, UI, and shader-flag changes did not establish a consistent improvement. The next useful investigation is a driver trace of command submission/waiting inside presentation, followed by a larger renderer change only when that trace supports it. A moving combat workload would also test performance beyond these stationary camera recordings.

    Why your live QSS-M FPS can be higher

    The chart measures first timedemos in fresh processes, not warmed live gameplay. Its discarded warm-up runs in a separate process. It warms OS/driver caches, but cannot preserve engine state for the measured passes. On the same PC and identical QSS-M executable, Aerowalk rose from 2,102 FPS on the first pass to 2,840 FPS at the repeat-pass median in one process.

    The benchmark's native settings query confirms r_shadows 0 and r_outline 0, with scene caching on its automatic default. The first-pass penalty also appears with scene caching disabled, so scene-cache construction alone does not explain it. Demo reloads reset scene caches. These checks demonstrate a warm-process effect; they do not identify a specific driver, shader, or CPU-cache cost.

    QSS-M only · Aerowalk · FPS · eight passes in each process

    The saved main config uses r_fastsky 2, r_waterwarp 0, and r_drawflame 0. Applying those three together produced no clear uplift in this sweep. Its outlines and shadows are enabled, unlike the benchmark. Both 4K conditions had a verified 3840 × 2160 client area.

    Live FPS counts rendered frames over about 0.75 seconds. Timedemo processes the recorded network messages at accelerated speed, with this demo advancing one packet per rendered frame after signon. The turning view and demo-decoding workload differ from live movement, so 2,500+ live FPS is compatible with a lower timedemo result. Conditions here ran sequentially with one session each; ranges overlap and this is not a controlled estimate of each setting's isolated cost. Supplemental QSS-M results are excluded from the six-engine ranking. A warmed-game ranking would require the same revised procedure for every engine.

    Presentation is the strongest measured lead

    A private source build measured ordinary demo playback, skipped 3,000 rendered frames, then aggregated five seconds. At 800 × 600 windowed, approximately 198 µs per frame elapsed inside SDL_GL_SwapWindow, compared with 85 µs in rendering/HUD submission. In the fullscreen probe the swap interval fell to 125 µs. That interval includes driver work and potential waits for the GPU; GPU timestamps are needed to separate rendering from presentation overhead. The sample covers part of the turn and is not comparable to a full timedemo score.

    Optimization priorities

    1. Separate GPU rendering from present waits. Add asynchronous GPU timestamps to the isolated profiler, compare matched windowed/fullscreen runs at 800 × 600 and 4K, then optimize the measured source of waiting or GPU work. Preserve image quality and verify frame-time distributions.
    2. Remove repeated HUD resource lookups. The CPU stack sample finds SCR_ShowObsFrags searching for optional gfx/ibar2.lmp every rendered frame. The file lookup path accounts for about 5% of sampled time during normal playback. Cache the loaded or missing result and invalidate it through SCR_LoadPics on HUD/game reload. A short scr_obsitems 0 timedemo probe did not show a clear gain, so this is confirmed redundant work, not a proven explanation for the throughput gap.
    3. Measure demo processing separately. Timedemo accelerates packet parsing and rewind-state tracking; normal playback receives far fewer recorded messages per rendered frame. Optimize measured decoder/snapshot costs while preserving normal rewind behavior, and validate live gameplay alongside timedemo.
    4. Recheck all nine maps and all engines. Use the same in-process warm-up, matched rendering features, 800 × 600 plus 4K, and rotating engine order. Retain the existing launch/first-use results as a separate metric. Leading one view does not establish a lead across maps or workloads.

    The optimized MSVC build also did not show a clear compiler-only improvement over the installed executable. The remaining gap has not been traced to one definitive engine defect. Those first diagnostic runs preceded the observer HUD cache change reported above; they did not replace the installed binary.

    FPS method, settings, and limitations

    Identical protocol-15 NetQuake demos recorded in QSS-M: a stationary camera turning approximately 360° over 20 seconds at the first deathmatch spawn on each map. Stock id1 game code, no monsters or active players. CTF maps test their geometry and stock entities; CTF gameplay is absent. This view samples one spawn and its visible surfaces, not the whole map.

    One engine runs at a time. Every map/engine combination receives one discarded warm-up and five native timedemo measurements, with engine order rotated between passes. The run resumed after configuration checks; replacement ezQuake samples for some early maps were collected separately. Diagnostic samples are excluded. Each pass starts a fresh process; startup and map loading are excluded by the engine's timedemo timer. OS file and driver shader caches stay warm. The runner stops its owned process after the result has been written. Background throttling is disabled through native engine controls; Quakespasm-family clients use -listen -noudp to bypass their focus sleep without UDP networking. No active server or match is running.

    800 × 600 physical client area, checked directly for all six engines; FOV 90, view size 100, VSync off, MSAA off, and uncapped requested FPS. Sound enabled. Same pak0/pak1 and BSP bytes; no personal .lit, .ent, replacement textures, or model packs. vkQuake uses Vulkan; the other engines use OpenGL. Renderer defaults, interpolation, particles, audio sampling/buffers, and internal timing paths differ, so image quality and workload are not perfectly identical. Native timedemo frame counts and timing precision are retained in the samples.

    “ms / frame” is 1000 / FPS, an average-throughput equivalent. These tests do not measure 1% lows, stutter, input latency, or network play. Five passes show repeatability, not statistical significance. Cross-map summaries use the geometric mean of each map's median FPS, weighting all nine maps equally. All six engines also receive the lifecycle tests above. Protocol and server differences for joining are described in the lifecycle methodology.

    How lifecycle time was measured

    Six engines, one local machine, five rotating rounds. All six lifecycle datasets were measured again under this setup. Earlier two-engine lifecycle results and pilot attempts are excluded from these summaries. The 324 existing FPS passes remain unchanged. FTE lifecycle sessions were repeated with its native -noupdates option after an update-source prompt was confirmed; prior FTE attempts are excluded.
    Timing endpoints and comparable workloads
    • Engine start: Process creation to the native BENCH_READY command-readiness marker, with no map loaded.
    • Launch → first map: A separate fresh process loading start immediately; process creation to completed client signon. This measures the combined path directly.
    • Initial map load: The first map start command in an already-started fresh process, immediately before the command to completed client signon. Startup and menu settling are excluded.
    • Subsequent map load: map e1m1 after start has completed signon in the same process; immediate command marker to completed client signon. Common assets are already cached.
    • Connect · local server: A fresh client settles at the menu, then joins e1m1 on loopback. Immediate connect-command marker to completed client signon. Five NetQuake clients use one QSS-M server; ezQuake uses an FTE QuakeWorld server.
    • Connect · Denver: Fresh client joining denver.quakeone.com:26000 on aerowalk. Immediate hostname connect-command marker to native signon stage 4. Same preinstalled map and custom sounds; server empty before each attempt. ezQuake cannot join this NetQuake server.
    • Engine quit: The marker immediately before native quit to observed process exit, after e1m1 is loaded locally. Connection-session quit is excluded. Native console quit bypasses confirmation menus.

    Completed client signon is the native CL_SignonReply: 4 event for NetQuake clients. ezQuake uses its native f_spawn alias executed after CL_MakeActive; this includes its shader-program preparation and the next command-buffer service. These are observable client-readiness milestones, not measurements of the first displayed pixel.

    Same QSS-M NetQuake server for QSS-M, FTE, Ironwail, vkQuake, and QSS. ezQuake joins an FTE QuakeWorld server; its protocol and server workload differ, so no cross-protocol winner is claimed.

    Sessions, caches, settings, and scheduling

    Each engine has five lifecycle sessions (ready → start → e1m1 → quit), five independent fresh launches directly into start, and five independent fresh menu-to-server connection sessions. Engine order rotates between rounds. Isolated portable copies use identical stock pak0/pak1 bytes, 800 × 600 verified physical client area, FOV 90, VSync/MSAA off, sound on, and requested 144 FPS limits. OS file and driver caches remain warm; this is not a reboot or cold-storage benchmark.

    Engine-native frame waits settle between actions; FTE uses deferred in timers because map changes clear queued commands. ezQuake's startup flush ignores waits, so native serverexec stages and f_spawn callbacks schedule its actions after initialization. Settling is excluded from command-to-ready timings. The ezQuake readiness marker runs in its native runtime buffer after queued renderer configuration; five replacement lifecycle sessions were collected separately after this endpoint audit. Their original attempts are excluded and retained in the raw evidence. Quakespasm-family clients use -listen 8 to suppress focus sleep, with UDP enabled and the client explicitly bound to loopback; deathmatch and coop are disabled. Native renderer/network scheduling still differs. Local connection sessions target the isolated servers. Denver sessions target the public server after untimed permission-dialog setup, with no player input during timing. Native auxiliary-file requests are included: ezQuake requests a missing base skin, and QSS-M may request missing location files; the local server's missing-file responses remain part of joining. FTE uses native -noupdates so update prompts do not block its sessions. Other background release/add-on checks may still occur under shipped defaults.

    NetQuake local servers use vanilla protocol 15 (including vkQuake's verified sv_protocol Base-15 setting). The hidden QSS-M dedicated connection server runs e1m1 at 127.0.0.1:26001. The separate hidden FTE QuakeWorld server serves the same stock game data at 127.0.0.1:27501. Released engine packages retain bundled assets and built-in map/entity fixes; these can differ between engines. Rendering uses Vulkan in vkQuake and OpenGL in the others.

    The host clock is Python perf_counter. Native logs are polled every 1 ms; OS scheduling and console flushing add measurement uncertainty. Medians and observed min–max ranges describe only these five local runs. Quit ends at actual process exit. Commands, configurations, hashes, every observed event, and exit codes are retained in the raw JSON.

    Denver connection setup and cleanup

    Fresh process, menu settle, hostname connect command to native signon stage 4. Same preinstalled BSP and custom sound bytes, warm OS/DNS caches. Protocol extensions disabled where supported: base NetQuake/FitzQuake networking. Real public network/server behavior and native retries included. No player chat or input. Five rounds with rotated engine order. User-authorized cmd dm normal aerowalk fixed the map before collection. Player count must return to zero before every launch; map status checked before and after. Native post-signon quit callbacks in QSS-M and FTE, owned-process termination otherwise; cleanup is excluded from connect timing and no public-session quit metric is measured. ezQuake omitted because the server is NetQuake and ezQuake live networking is QuakeWorld. On resumption, map identity is fixed to aerowalk rather than adopting the current rotation. Affected rotated-map attempts are excluded. Owned source-port disconnect datagrams are used after termination when needed; endpoint ownership is retained per row.

    Server: CRMod 7 on QSS-M 1.6.9-1aa5a7d. Target uses explicit port 26000; FTE uses native connectnq. All five compatible clients received identical aerowalk BSP and 35 cached custom sound files. The main command buffer stays empty during signon, allowing server handshake commands to execute. Protocol settings and cleanup differ from the local sessions and are retained in each raw row. Connection timing ends before cleanup; public-server quit time is not measured.

    Server status, map, player counts, resource hashes, configurations, native events, and logs are retained in the raw JSON. ezQuake remains benchmarked on the compatible local QuakeWorld server.
